metadata.methods_description: Children with reading or math difficulties underwent psychometric testing (spelling, reading speed, comprehension, general math knowledge, arithmetic hits and reaction time, selective attention, IQ) and EEG recording in a PRE-intervention session and a POST-intervention session three months later. EEG included a 3-minute eyes-open resting state and either reading aloud with comprehension questions or two blocks of 20 arithmetic operations. Participants were randomly assigned to an experimental group (Smartick use for three months) or a control group.

citation_details.title: Enhancing learning skills in children by using assistive technology: a psychophysiological database
citation_details.author: César E. Corona-González, Luz María Alonso-Valerdi, David I. Ibarra-Zárate, Fabiola Reveca Gómez-Velázquez
citation_details.abstract: OBJECTIVES: The present dataset provides psychometric and electroencephalographic information from children with either reading or math difficulties. This data was collected before and after children utilized Smartick, an assistive technology that boosts reading and math proficiency. This dataset aims to understand how assistive technology can support learning in children. DATA DESCRIPTION: Seventy-six Mexican children aged 7 to 13 were recruited for this study. Every child underwent a psychometric assessment to identify learning difficulties. Then, each child was categorized within the group of reading difficulties or math difficulties. After that, children underwent electroencephalographic recording in two conditions: (1) resting state and (2) while performing reading or math activities. Each child was reallocated to (1) the experimental subgroup, which interacted with Smartick, and (2) the control subgroup, which did not enroll in the intervention. Finally, psychometric and electroencephalographic (EEG) data were collected again after a three-month follow-up period. All electroencephalographic recordings are presented in set format. The authors also share different .xlsx files describing: (1) psychometric results throughout the study, (2) the availability of electroencephalographic data, event list within the electroencephalographic recordings during (3) reading activities and (4) math activities, and (5) the engagement percentage with Smartick in the experimental group.

citation_details.title: Baseline resting-state EEG and individual differences in academic gains among children with reading and mathematics difficulties
citation_details.author: Yu Sun
citation_details.abstract: This project examines whether baseline resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) explains individual differences in academic gains among children with reading or mathematics difficulties who took part in a three-month digital learning programme. It is a preregistered secondary analysis of a public dataset (OpenNeuro ds006260, version 1.0.1, CC0), which contains pre- and post-intervention psychometric scores and 32-channel resting-state EEG from 76 Mexican children aged 7 to 13. Children were assigned to a reading or a mathematics strand and, within each strand, to a digital intervention arm (Smartick, an adaptive online programme used for three months) or a control arm that continued usual instruction. The study is motivated by a simple observation: mean intervention effects in this literature are modest, whereas variability between children is large. Some children improve substantially over three months; others do not. Behavioural predictors such as baseline attainment, IQ and attention account for only part of this variability. Resting-state EEG is brief, inexpensive and well tolerated by children, and has been proposed as a scalable marker of learning potential, but no study has examined it in children receiving home-based digital instruction across both reading and mathematics. We ask four questions. First, do baseline EEG features - posterior relative alpha, frontal theta/beta ratio, the aperiodic exponent of the power spectrum, alpha peak frequency, and central-parietal low beta - predict the magnitude of gain, after adjustment for age, sex, IQ, baseline performance and selective attention? Second, are these associations domain-specific; that is, do reading and mathematics gains have different EEG predictors? Third, does the strength of the association differ between the intervention and control arms? Fourth, do baseline features predict change in the same features over three months, and is that change associated with behavioural gain? We do not test intervention efficacy. Re-analysis of the public psychometric file shows no significant group-by-time interaction on any outcome, and allocation was semi-random. The research question therefore concerns individual differences in gain, with intervention arm modelled as a moderator rather than as a treatment contrast. Analyses use scale-invariant EEG features, because the stored amplitude scale differs across files by roughly three orders of magnitude; peak-based alpha frequency is supplemented by spectral parameterisation (FOOOF) because alpha peaks are undetectable in about 40% of recordings. Primary models are covariate-adjusted linear regressions with heteroscedasticity-consistent errors, false-discovery-rate control, bootstrap confidence intervals and Bayes factors for null results, followed by ten prespecified robustness checks. Out-of-sample prediction is examined as an exploratory analysis. Expected outcomes are a medium-sized association of posterior alpha and of the aperiodic exponent with literacy gain, and a weaker, possibly mathematics-specific association for central beta. Null results will be reported with Bayes factors rather than interpreted as an absence of effect. The project will produce a manuscript for a peer-reviewed journal, together with analysis code, a participant-level feature table and an inclusion log. The dataset is de-identified and released under CC0. The original study was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of the Institute of Neuroscience, Universidad de Guadalajara (ET122022-356) and registered as ISRCTN14013636. No new data will be collected. In the interest of transparency: the dataset is public and was inspected before this registration. The registration documents exactly which analyses were and were not conducted beforehand. The hypothesis linking posterior alpha to reading-speed gain is therefore labelled a discovery, whereas the hypotheses concerning mathematics, domain specificity, incremental validity of the aperiodic component and neural change are confirmatory.
